top_story: The conflict widened sharply after U.S. forces sank five Iranian oil tankers, prompting Tehran on 9 September to launch its largest declared shipping retaliation yet near the Strait of Hormuz and later claim strikes on more than a dozen vessels. This maritime escalation followed the Houthis’ 8 September attacks on four Saudi cities and oil facilities, which wounded more than 70 people and opened a second pressure point on Gulf energy infrastructure and civilian centers. Oil prices moving above $100 per barrel reflect not only disrupted shipping lanes but a growing perception that Iran and its partners can impose costs across the region faster than Washington and Riyadh can contain them. The immediate trajectory points toward a broader war of economic coercion in which civilian insecurity and energy market shock are becoming central instruments, not side effects.
